storyline.arc: It started as an empty repo and, in twelve commits, had an embedded terminal, token counting and commit message generation. Then came the long middle: making it work with both Claude and OpenCode, running many sessions at once, sharing whole sessions through git, and a summarizer that kept quoting its own instructions back at you. Along the way it picked up CI, a docs landing page, a metrics dashboard with zoomable charts, a Linux bubblewrap sandbox, and five releases. It ended up as aGiTrack: renamed, published, per-session branches, and still occasionally arguing with a screenshot.

This is the big bang episode: two "Initial version" commits back to back, then ten more that pile on everything the tool needs to be usable. Over 5,000 lines land in one sitting across `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, `pyproject.toml`, and a growing test folder.

The shape of the product shows up in the commit titles. `f207887` swaps in a tmux-like embedded terminal, `1b5806d` gets token counting into shape, and `b6462f6` starts the long-running project of making commit messages not terrible. Then `a3fa83d` adds status checks and a commit dialog box, which is the moment this stops being a script and starts being an app.

The last two are the classic end-of-day cleanup: `5755494` improves OpenCode session parsing and `6a9fa8e` fixes CLI colors. Tests arrive alongside, with `test_proxy.py`, `test_state.py`, `test_commit_message.py`, `test_opencode_parse.py`, and `test_opencode_session.py` all showing up in the same push.

`ced9b84` is the load-bearing commit here: a major refactor to support both Claude and OpenCode instead of just one. New test files appear that tell you exactly what the shape of the abstraction is, `test_claude_session.py` next to the existing OpenCode tests, plus `test_backends_and_config.py`.

And yes, `03e9d15` improves commit messages again. That is now twice in two episodes. Some features are never quite done.

`2f38733` adds multi-session support, and the rest of the episode is the fallout from that in the best way. `a1396a4` improves how multiple sessions are handled and `2522df1` sorts out branch management across sessions, because once you have several agents working at once, the question of which branch each one lives on stops being theoretical.

The supporting cast is doing real work too. `adabc98` fixes a scrolling issue, `84c3d89` improves UI rendering, and `546b898` improves metadata and descriptions so you can tell your sessions apart at a glance. Roughly 5,000 lines move in one day.

New tests show the widening blast radius: `test_worktree.py` and `test_lock.py` both appear, which is a strong hint that concurrent sessions brought worktrees and locking along as required reading.

`f641579` is a nearly 1,900 line stability push that spreads tests into new corners: `test_cli.py`, `test_shell.py`, and `test_sandbox.py` all join the suite alongside the existing proxy, lock, and session tests. This is the sitting where the project stops adding surface and starts hardening what is there.

Then `53abb5a` catches a very specific, very annoying real-world case. The prompt spells it out: starting aGiT from an empty git-initialized directory threw an error and the tool would not start. The developer also asked for tests to prove it stays fixed, and there was a second complaint in the same breath about what the global config was showing. The fix is small, 100 lines, and touches `test_cli.py`, `test_state.py`, and `test_backends_and_config.py`.

Worth noting the prompt opens with a context-window continuation summary. The stability work had gotten long enough that the conversation itself ran out of room.

chapters.detail:
`570d02a` bundles three related things: worktree recovery, sandbox support, and general session improvements. Worktree recovery is the natural sequel to the multi-session work from earlier, since once you create worktrees automatically you eventually have to clean up after the ones that got left behind. `uv.lock` and `pyproject.toml` both move, so dependencies shifted here too.

`65ec499` follows with better staging handling and, you guessed it, improved commit messages. That is the fourth separate commit in this history dedicated to making commit messages better. For a tool whose whole job is recording how people build software, obsessing over the commit message is arguably the point.

Tests land across `test_claude_session.py`, `test_opencode_session.py`, `test_proxy.py`, and `test_worktree.py`, keeping both backends covered as the new behavior goes in.
chapters.summary: Two PRs add worktree recovery and sandbox support, then clean up how staging works and, once again, how commit messages read.

chapters.detail:
The headline here is LLM-based summarization: commits now carry a written summary so the design context behind a change survives past the diff. It gets documented in the README right after, twice, because the feature is only useful if people know it exists.

Around it, a batch of ergonomics work. Unrecognized CLI args now get forwarded to the backend instead of being rejected, a `--no-worktree` option lands, and mypy errors get burned down in four small modules to chip away at the baseline. Then `scripts/check.sh` plus a pre-push hook mirror what CI does, so failures show up before the push rather than after.

The closing commit is the interesting one: backend-made commits get trace and metadata attached by amending them. The prompt is blunt about the goal. That amend trick is what makes it possible to record what an agent did without changing how the agent commits.

chapters.detail:
The prompts here are refreshingly direct: go read the latest comments on issues 8, 35, 56 and 14, find what was not actually fixed, and fix them one by one. That is exactly what happens. Summarization becomes non-blocking so it no longer stalls the commit, and the summary is promoted to the leading paragraph of the message. Unusable summaries get detected so the trace stops repeating prompts. Summarizer backends get moved to a scratch cwd so they never run inside the session worktree, which is the kind of bug you only find once.

A second prompt is pure attention to detail: the covered commits list showed some short hashes and one long one, and the interaction trace was out of order. Both get fixed. Then the `<agent>` tag becomes `<aGiT>` on amended backend commits, configurable via `tag_backend_commits`, so the tool signs its work under its own name.

The docs get a pass too, with em dashes stripped from the landing page copy and the tab title shortened to `aGiT · agent + git`. And the last commit is a real one: a privacy warning at startup that has to be acknowledged. A tool that records prompts and commits should say so out loud before it starts recording.

This stretch started with the developer going back to read the unfinished comments on four open issues and asking the agent to fix them one by one, with tests where needed. Out came a batch of small but very visible things: the status bar now shows the agent's working directory (and then, after a second look, the base repo path instead of the worktree path), every `<agent>` tag became `<aGiT>` including in the tests and popup messages, and the covered-commits metadata stopped mixing one long hash in with the short ones.

The bigger one was session naming. Restarting aGiT only kept the last session, so the developer pushed for names to be preserved across runs and linked back to the right backend session. Related to that, the commit and summarization popups now say which session they belong to, which sounds tiny until you have three sessions and no idea which one just committed.

Along the way came a scripted JSON mode (`--prompt`) and a runnable `scripts/demo.sh`, plus a fix for issue #58 about merge commits sweeping up every changed file. The privacy warning even got a blank line above it. Tests landed in `test_proxy.py`, `test_backend_commits.py`, `test_commit_message.py` and `test_cli.py`.

chapters.detail:
The big one: v0.0.1. This episode brought a dashboard, auto-update, and `scripts/publish.sh` to handle the release. The script did not survive first contact with reality. Branch protection meant it could not merge straight into main, so it was reworked to open a PR at the end instead. Then the PyPI description turned out to be too long and had an image that never rendered, so that got trimmed, and the developer asked for a way to bump major and minor versions rather than only the patch.

Base-branch switching was crashing aGiT outright. The fix went further than the crash: new sessions should now always start from whatever branch is actually checked out in the directory, instead of assuming a default.

The tail end is pure terminal archaeology. Escape was not working, so the developer added handling for kitty terminal encodings and support for the kitty keyboard protocol for the menu key and Escape. One commit in that run is titled simply `.`, which is the most honest commit message in the repo.

thoughts.quote: The publish script should create a PR at the end instead of attempting to merge directly, because branch protection rules disallow merging into the main branch without PR.

thoughts.note: A crash on base-branch switching exposed a deeper assumption: sessions were not starting from the branch actually checked out.
thoughts.quote: When switching base branch in agit, it quits with an error. Also, new sessions should always be started with the current checked-out branch in the directory. When the directory has checked-out a different branch and an aGiT session is on a different branch, prompt the user whether they would like to switch to the new branch in the directory. If they don't switch, still merge into the original branch, but care needs to be taken since the directory is on a different branch.

chapters.detail:
This sitting started with the kind of bugs you only find by using your own tool. The aGiT command palette was cutting items off at the bottom because the box was too small, so the menu got resized. Exiting aGiT sometimes threw a `FileNotFoundError` from deep inside subprocess launching, and that intermittent crash got tracked down and fixed. The dashboard also learned to count tokens once instead of double-counting them in squashed merges.

Then the terminal saga continued. Earlier it was kitty that had opinions about Escape; this time iTerm2 on Mac was quietly passing Ctrl-C and Ctrl-G straight through to the backend agent instead of letting aGiT catch them. The fix had to work with both the kitty protocol and iTerm2's, which is the sort of requirement that only exists because the developer uses both.

The other half of the episode was shipping infrastructure: `release-patch.yml` and `release-tag.yml` for automated PyPI and GitHub releases. The first version pushed straight to main, which is exactly what branch protection exists to prevent, so it was reworked to create a PR and merge that instead. And of course `ruff format` had opinions about `tests/test_dashboard.py`, so CI got its formatting fix too.
chapters.summary: A run of small but sharp fixes (menu too small, Ctrl-C swallowed by iTerm, FileNotFoundError on quit) lands alongside automated PyPI and GitHub release workflows that had to be taught to open a PR instead of pushing to main.

v0.0.2 went out, the README got restructured, and then a nagging detail got cleaned up: the aGiT version stored in commit metadata did not match the installed version, because two hand-maintained version sources existed (`version` in `pyproject.toml` and one elsewhere). One source of truth, problem gone.

The big addition was an activity-over-time plot: tokens, code lines and commit counts on the same chart, toggleable, and respecting the existing filters. Then came the natural follow-ups that only appear once you look at real data. You need to zoom the x-axis to see different time ranges. Zooming by dragging is annoying, so add a SHOW dropdown with look-back presets. Switching filters should not wipe the SHOW and PER fields you just set. And the from/to range showed a single day when the data actually spanned the full history, so that got corrected too.

On the commit message side, Markdown headings inside user and agent messages now get automatically incremented so they nest under the Agent heading instead of fighting it, and the dashboard commit log renders the different levels distinctly. One commit even got used as its own test case: the developer pointed the agent at `f14c46c` and said, look, the Agent heading is level two, so these should be deeper. There was also a merge-timing fix so a commit merges automatically after creation rather than waiting on the agent's reply to a new prompt.

chapters.detail:
It started simply: "Now, work on this issue https://github.com/core-aix/agit/issues/55". The result was full Claude session sharing through git, with a note that OpenCode sessions were not supported yet, plus a CI fix for what turned out to be a test-only bug.

Then the real questions started, and they were all the good kind. How do I know the session was shared, I don't see it on GitHub? Do new updates share automatically? That produced opt-in auto-share and a "Manage sessions" view. But auto-update made the terminal crawl, so background work got pushed off the main thread. Then Manage Shared Sessions still took a few seconds to open, and turning on auto-update made a shared session disappear from the dashboard entirely. Two more rounds of performance and resilience fixes followed.

The developer also worried about GitHub itself: sync on commit rather than on a timer, and stop the dashboard fetching so often. Auto-share was decoupled from its background timer. Later came the practical stuff: auto-update state that survives across aGiT runs, the session list showing which sessions are shared, a two-machine alternating workflow, immediate deletion of older session versions instead of waiting for garbage collection, and one update fired straight away when auto-update is enabled.

Tucked in among all that: the dashboard filter bar became a single frozen row, the scope field went away because it duplicated committer, and from/to collapsed into one custom period selector.

chapters.detail:
This sitting started small and petty: the random session names were pulling words nobody had ever said out loud, so `0d73690` swapped them for plain common nouns. Then the developer asked the agent to double-check the whole branch, concurrent session and sharing logic, and that turned up real problems: dangling branches and deferred prompts in `28e5a05`, and a race condition in the deferred merge prompt in `d794805`.

The sharpest fix was `ff6270d`. The branch switch dialog was popping up before the session's changes had merged back into the original branch, which is exactly the wrong order. Now it waits for the merge, unless the session was cancelled, in which case switching is fine. To prove the rest held up, `f2c6e69` built end-to-end tests on a throwaway repo with real branches, exercising switching and merging directly. That work shipped as PR #81 and then `3c2e878` cut Release v0.0.6.

After the release the focus moved to numbers. Token counts are the whole point of aGiTrack, so the developer wanted them exact for both Claude and OpenCode: `69d9637` added sub-agent token accounting for cases the repo did not even have yet, `41b0a13` killed a deduplication bug found with the same temp-repo test trick, and `1ef611a` started recording compactions and session forks or copies in the interaction trace, since both move token usage around. `46608c7` closed out two nagging details: a summary input token stuck at 20, and a wrong agitrack version in the metadata.

Along the way `63d1b42` answered a different worry entirely, whether aGiTrack behaves in various terminals on Mac, Windows and Linux, by adding an OS matrix and terminal compatibility testing.

thoughts.note: They spotted that the branch switch prompt was racing ahead of the merge, and worked out that a cancelled session is the one case where switching early is safe.
thoughts.quote: The branch switching dialog after a running session finishes should happen after the changes are merged into the original branch, not before. If a session is cancelled, the user can feel free to switch branches for that session.

thoughts.note: Deciding that token counts are too important to trust by eye, they reused the temp-repo test approach to prove the numbers exactly for both backends.

The session opened with a small efficiency ask: the summarizer was burning the default thinking level when it did not need to. One commit later it runs with the lowest thinking on both backends. Then came the bigger question, and the developer was blunt about it: auto-update should not depend on the system's package manager, and if that is impossible, then enumerate every package manager there is. The answer landed in `AGENTS.md` as a design note plus a fallback routing path, with special care for people who installed via pip rather than from source.

The follow-up was about failure. If the update breaks, catch the exception, tell the user how to update by hand, and let them keep using the older aGiTrack. That is the polite version of "do not brick someone's tool." In the same breath the developer spotted a bug in their own earlier commit: a stray `/comp` slash command was leaking into the captured user message, which the interaction header already covered. Slash commands now get filtered uniformly in `agitrack/transcripts/claude.py` and `opencode.py`. The footer line calling the intro page "a git log" was cut too.

After v0.0.8 shipped, the second half went after commit message quality. Reasoning effort and thinking level now land in aGiTrack metadata when available. Then four features were requested one by one, the first being an option to put *all* the agent's messages to the user into the commit message instead of only the last one, plus cancellation handling and session naming. That first feature got a `--full-agent-messages` CLI flag so it can be flipped per run rather than only in config. v0.0.9 closed it out.

chapters.detail:
This episode is one long argument with a terminal. VS Code likes to help: it activates your Python venv, it splits editors, it sends `source [PATH]` into whatever is running. The problem is that whatever is running was aGiTrack, and then the agent backend, which meant a bare `source [PATH]` was landing in the middle of a conversation. `74d3f60` restored shell-based launch sequencing so that command goes to the shell first, before aGiTrack starts.

Along the way the developer got curious about their own extension and asked which functions in `extension.ts` came from the VS Code template and which the agent had written, and which exact line spawns the terminal. That kind of question tends to precede real fixes, and it did: a startup progress notification (`021796d`), then a fix so the toast waits for actual startup instead of vanishing (`fe68358`), then an early "aGiTrack is starting..." print in the CLI itself so it shows up even outside the extension (`2bea883`).

The harder half was shutdown. `a62dce8` added a promise with a 60s timeout in `deactivate()` plus a dialog telling people to use Ctrl-G then exit for a clean stop. `f13a8da` went further and put recovery in the Extension Host: if the terminal dies abruptly, check the transcript, merge only if the turn finished and there is no conflict, never merge an aborted turn. Then `e952ac9` and `8c8d2e8` added a settings option for CLI args and stopped the split editor button from spawning a second empty terminal.

The last three commits are the tail chasing its own bugs. `4554df7` fixed three regressions at once: the extension could not be reopened after exiting, the venv switch came back and its Enter skipped the privacy warning, and launching from the extension sometimes killed an aGiTrack already running in the terminal. `049b9e4` made shell integration wait for the venv activation, and `221a92e` finally disabled venv activation during launch outright, after the developer pasted the exact terminal output showing a `^C` killing aGiTrack right before the venv switch.
chapters.summary: A full sitting of wrestling VS Code's terminal into behaving: startup notifications that wait, graceful shutdown with a 60s timeout, a recovery path for abrupt closes, and finally killing the venv activation that was sending Ctrl-C into a running aGiTrack.

thoughts.note: They worked out that cleanup cannot live in the terminal at all, and moved commits and merges into the Extension Host with careful rules about aborted turns and conflicts.
thoughts.quote: It seems the best approach is to have an Extension Host that handles remaining cleanups such as commits and merges if the terminal itself is closed abruptly.

thoughts.note: Pasting the raw terminal output showing a ^C followed by the venv switch was the moment the real culprit stopped being guesswork.
thoughts.quote: No, look at what happens now. A ^C is sent to kill the aGiTrack process and then venv is switched: agitrack % agitrack && exit aGiTrack is starting... WARNING: aGiTrack records the conversation in git commit messages — every message you enter in the chat can become part of the repository history. Do not enter passwords, API keys, or other sensitive information in the chat. (Keeping secrets out of prompts is good practice anyway.) Press Enter to acknowledge and continue (q to quit): ^C aGiTrack not started. agitrack % source [PATH] (agit) agitrack %

thoughts.note: Three regressions landed at once, which is the usual price of fixing terminal lifecycle bugs one at a time.
thoughts.quote: Please continue with your edits. Your recent edits broke a lot of things. First, the extension cannot be reopened after exiting anymore. Second, the venv switch appeared again and that enter skipped the privacy warning. Third, starting aGiTrack from the extension sometimes automatically quits the running aGiTrack in the terminal. This should never happen.

chapters.detail:
The ask was simple to say and annoying to build: Esc should move up one level, from any menu item, at any depth. `33cf623` took a first swing. Then the follow-up was blunt: the sessions menu still exits fully, and even two levels deep Esc still returns straight to the agent. `61330b8` and `1b914fa` kept going until it landed as a three-signal return model in `agitrack/proxy/modal.py`, which is the kind of thing you only build once you have failed the simple version twice.

Then the new problem: it worked but felt bad. Too much delay going back to a parent menu, and "closed" popups flashing before the parent reappeared. `e8f1f30` and `c5d6540` refactored the menu to back-step smoothly and wrap content properly. Somewhere in there the tests ran so long they became the bug, and the instruction was to stop and rethink the approach: `e54dce0` killed an infinite test loop and made the feedback cycle fast again.

Small but sharp: `502bb0e` removed Ctrl-C as the menu cancel key, because Ctrl-C quits aGiTrack, which is a fairly loud way to close a menu. `cce546f` renamed the exit option to "exit aGiTrack" so nobody confused it with leaving the menu. Docs got the same treatment: `716fefc` deleted the long-dead READ ONLY TUI mode from `docs/user-flow.md`, and `37dae6c` then `f8979a8` fought with mermaid click directives that opened blank pages before giving up and using plain Markdown anchor links, which work.
chapters.summary: A long back-and-forth to make Esc walk up the menu tree instead of dumping you back to the agent, ending in a three-signal return model and a menu that stopped feeling sluggish.

thoughts.note: Accepting that per-menu patches were not enough and a single explicit return model was needed for Esc to behave everywhere.

commits.subject: <aGiTrack> Implement idle backoff to pause background polling when aGiTrack is inactive
<aGiTrack> Raise minimum poll interval to 1s with smart timeout calculation for interactive responsiveness.
<aGiTrack> Idle backoff reduces energy use while preserving responsiveness

chapters.detail:
This sitting started with a very concrete complaint: the Mac was pointing fingers about energy use. The ask was simple, pause background tasks and checks when the user hasn't typed into the aGiTrack terminal for a while and no session is active. That became idle backoff in `agitrack/proxy/runner.py`, with new knobs in `agitrack/config/settings.py` and tests in `tests/test_proxy.py`.

Then came the follow-up review of the numbers themselves. A 0.2 second active poll interval looked absurd on inspection, so the floor was raised to 1 second with smarter timeout calculation, plus a nudge to stop brute-force walking every file and folder. Fast enough to feel interactive, slow enough to stop cooking the laptop.

The rules were written down in `AGENTS.md` so the next round of work would not quietly undo them. There was also a small side quest about hyperlinks in the workflows opening blank pages, fixed by pointing at sections inside the same Markdown file.
chapters.summary: After macOS started blaming VS Code for eating battery, the polling loop learned to back off when nobody is typing and no session is running.

thoughts.note: The battery warning from macOS turned a vague performance worry into a concrete requirement: no background polling when the terminal is idle and nothing is running.
thoughts.quote: aGiTrack should pause background tasks/checks when the user didn't type into the aGiTrack terminal for some time and there is no active session running. This should save the battery. On Mac, it was saying that VS Studio is consuming significant energy when aGiTrack runs inside it; that warning was gone after quitting aGiTrack.

thoughts.note: Reading their own config and deciding 0.2 seconds was indefensible, they set a hard 1 second floor rather than micro-tuning.
thoughts.quote: ACTIVE_POLL_SECONDS (0.2s) sounds like a very small interval. No poll should be less than a second. Make sure that any file and folder checks are efficient too, instead of brute-forcelly checking though every file and folder. Only read parts of files and folders as needed. Use some list files function with last modified time if appropriate.

chapters.title: Teaching aGiTrack to nap: idle backoff and a 1-second poll floor

The exit path got the full treatment. First, a prompt on unexpected exit with a recovery option, then the same prompt when quitting from the menu while the agent is still running. But the reverse case mattered too: if everything is committed and merged, don't nag with a mysterious "Finalizing commits..." message. The result was exit finalization that names the actual work being done, and a rule that exit always confirms but only finalizes when there is something to finalize.

Along the way, git operations moved to a dedicated background thread so input stayed responsive, a real mystery got solved (aGiTrack somehow uninstalling itself after a VS Code restart), and small polish landed like a blank line before "File(s):" headers. One prompt asked for a full double-check of every user flow and exit path, which is why `docs/user-flow.md` got updated alongside `agitrack/proxy/runner.py`, `tests/test_proxy.py`, and the new `tests/test_proxy_modal.py`.

The second half was a detour into CI. It ended as a shared composite action in `.github/actions/ai-release-notes/action.yml`, wired into both `release-patch.yml` and `release-tag.yml`, with a deliberate choice: no fallback to `--generate-notes`, the release fails loudly with a reason if the API is unavailable.

chapters.detail:
The first half was about flexibility: people wrap their coding agents in their own scripts, so `agitrack/cli.py` got support for a fully custom backend launch command instead of just extra options. That immediately raised the obvious question the developer asked out loud: how does aGiTrack still know which backend it is, so it can find the transcripts? The answer was to keep the backend flag and warn on mismatch, then a follow-up made that warning a real y/n confirmation instead of a message you scroll past. Shipped as PR #102, then v0.1.4.

The dashboard cleanup came next and was very much a "this bugs me" list. First the junk labels: "unknown" backend and "<synthetic>" model were showing up in the by-backend and by-model sections and got filtered out. Then the big one in `agitrack/metrics/web.py`: subagent token counts were being treated as their own categories, when they should be an annotation on the main types, so the whole thing became hierarchical with "of which" lines, applied consistently across both backends.

After that it was pure polish, one prompt per irritation: align the "aGiTrack's own calls" line with the other "of which" rows, add "Note:" before the log-scale explanation, put a separator before the note since it applies to the whole column, and move the horizontal rules so they land after each main token type instead of in the confusing middle. The log scale itself got fixed too: the floor became the smallest real value instead of a fixed tiny number, so bars actually spread out, plus a "log" marker inside each bar to distinguish them from the plain scalar bars.

Two real bugs got swept up along the way: exit still hanging on "Finalizing..." for up to 30 seconds, the VS Code button opening two terminals when clicked twice at startup, and the shared-session timestamp claiming "1d ago" for a session shared minutes earlier.
chapters.summary: aGiTrack learned to run wrapped backend commands (with a confirmation prompt when the backend looks wrong), and the token dashboard was rebuilt into a hierarchical, log-scaled view over several rounds of nitpicking.

thoughts.note: They stopped to ask whether the backend could be inferred from a custom command at all, and settled on keeping the flag plus a mismatch warning.
thoughts.quote: aGiTrack would still need to know which backend is being used, so that session transcripts can be tracked. Do you extract that automatically from the backend command or does the user still need to specify the backend separately>

thoughts.note: The realization that subagent tokens are a slice of the main token types, not separate categories, is what turned the dashboard into a hierarchy.
thoughts.quote: The dashboard should categorize the token types better. For example, I believe the subagent* categories should be just an annotation of how much of each type of tokens were for subagents. For example, the input tokens should be a sum of the main agent and subagent tokens; the amount of subagent tokens should be just a subset of it. In the same way, we can probably put cache write as a subset of input too. There could be a view showing a hierarchy indicating which category includes which other category.

thoughts.note: Working out that a fixed tiny log minimum was squashing all the bars together, when the smallest real value would spread them out.
thoughts.quote: For the log scale in the token bars, the minimum value should be set to the smallest number in the list, instead of some very small fixed number. This should make the bar widths spread out as much as possible.

chapters.title: Custom launch commands, then a full redesign of the token dashboard

chapters.detail:
This is the sitting where the developer stopped babysitting the Windows work and said the quiet part out loud: "do the full end-to-end TUI bring-up and everything that remains. No need to ask for my confirmation." And then, for good measure, "That includes Phases 3 and 4." Two commits later native Windows support was marked complete and VM-validated against issue #118.

Then came the trust-but-verify phase. They asked for the exact command to run aGiTrack through the Windows VM so they could try it themselves, plus a sanity check and regression tests, which shook out a socket leak in the ConPTY bridge (`agitrack/proxy/platform/_winconsole.py`, `tests/test_windows_platform.py`). The questions kept getting more practical: is the vsix on Windows the same file as on Linux, how do you RDP in from a host terminal, and does `pip install agitrack` just work from a Windows prompt? That last one led to `firstPython` learning to try the `py` launcher, because Windows people often do not have a bare `python` on PATH.

The episode closes on two things that were not really about Windows at all. Install hints for missing git and backends got written for Mac, Linux, and Windows, since someone installing the VS Code extension cold has no idea what else they need. And a separate bug: commits were being summarized but not merged into the base repo if the user fired off a new prompt before the merge finished, so merge gating and Claude's mid-turn message ordering both got fixed.
chapters.summary: The Windows port went from "process layer works" to a full validated bring-up, with a ConPTY socket leak fixed, a `py` launcher fallback, and install hints for every OS.

thoughts.note: They handed over the remaining phases in one go and let the agent run the whole Windows bring-up without checkpoints.

chapters.detail:
The commit prompts came back, but only in a specific case: a subagent was running while the main agent waited, so the backend looked idle when it was not. The fix in `agitrack/backends/proxy_agents.py` and `agitrack/transcripts/claude.py` adds transcript mtime to idle detection, because a transcript that is still being written means somebody is still working.

Then a nastier one. Start in worktree mode, quit, restart in no-worktree mode, and Claude complained that the environment changed between sessions even though no prompt had been sent. A worktree branch was leaking across the mode switch, and `agitrack/proxy/runner.py` now cleans it up on resume.

Finally, the efficiency insights got a dose of nuance. Long feedback loops are not a problem if the agent is just waiting for background tasks. Rework hotspots only count when the same lines are added and deleted repeatedly, not when someone is legitimately building several features in one file. Both distinctions went into `agitrack/metrics/insights.py`, which is the difference between an insight and a nag.
chapters.summary: Idle detection learned to watch transcript mtime so subagent waits do not trigger commit prompts, a worktree branch leak got plugged, and rework detection got a lot more careful.

This started with a very specific complaint from a repo running aGiTrack in background auto-commit mode: the turn had finished, but the commits had not. Then it got worse. chapters.detail:
The numbers did not add up. The agent apparently blamed session restarts, and the developer pushed back: there were only a few restarts, so that cannot explain such a big difference. Then came the instruction that actually cracked it, to create a dummy repo, run a few agent turns with code edits, and compare the tokens in the commit messages against the tokens shown in backtrace.

That experiment paid off. The first commit fixed three independent correctness issues across both dashboards (2293b44), touching `agitrack/metrics/backtrace.py`, `agitrack/metrics/collect.py` and `agitrack/transcripts/types.py`.

The second was the big one: lost context watermarks were causing entire sessions to be re-exported, which inflated the counts enormously (5d5fcf2). Fixes landed in `agitrack/proxy/commit_engine.py`, `agitrack/config/state.py` and `agitrack/recovery.py`, with new coverage in `tests/test_commit_engine.py`. For a tool whose whole pitch is measuring how you build with agents, getting the token math right is not optional.
chapters.summary: Token counts in the commit messages and the backtrace dashboard disagreed by too much to explain away, so the developer sent the agent to build a test repo and prove it, uncovering three separate bugs plus a watermark bug that re-exported whole sessions.

thoughts.note: Refusing to accept restarts as the explanation and asking for a reproducible dummy repo is what turned a hand-wave into a real watermark bug.
thoughts.quote: There were only a few restarts, so that cannot explain such a big difference

chapters.detail:
The opening bug is a classic terminal trap: pasting multiple lines into the backend agent's terminal made aGiTrack read some line breaks as Enter, which then got applied to its own popup menu about new commits. So a paste could answer a question you never saw. That got fixed in `agitrack/proxy/modal.py` and friends.

Cover commit detection was also wrong. The developer noticed the last commit was marked as a cover commit even though the covered commits were PR-related and not agent work, so the logic learned to tell locally-created work from commits that just arrived from elsewhere. The old commit message was then edited to drop the 'covered' part.

Then the bigger pieces. Ctrl-Z with the Claude backend left the TUI in a state the developer could not get out of, so signal handling got made safe for both backends. And self-update landed in `agitrack/update/selfupdate.py` and `restart.py`, triggered by either the TUI or the daemon, with locking so multiple instances do not fight. The first pass made it opt-in, and the developer pushed back: it should be default on, with a global config option for anyone who wants it off.

The cleanup at the end was about honesty in the logs. A user message was showing up twice in the interaction trace, which turned out to be rewound messages the parser was not skipping, and the backtrace dashboard stopped showing user-only traces by combining empty prompts with their responses. Releases 0.5.18 and 0.5.19 came out of this.
